front_blocks.md: Define **halogenoalkane**.

back_blocks.md: A **halogenoalkane** is an alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by a **halogen** atom. They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary based on the substitution of the carbon bearing the halogen.

front_blocks.md: Name three routes by which halogenoalkanes can be produced.

back_blocks.md:
1. **Free-radical substitution** of alkanes with Cl<sub>2</sub> or Br<sub>2</sub> in UV light.
2. **Electrophilic addition** of HX or X<sub>2</sub> to alkenes.
3. **Substitution** of an alcohol using HX, PCl<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub> or SOCl<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: What is the major product rule when HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene to form a halogenoalkane?

back_blocks.md: The major product has Br bonded to the **most substituted** carbon (**Markovnikov's rule**). This is because the more substituted carbon gives the more stable **carbocation** intermediate.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Electrophilic addition of a halogen (X<sub>2</sub>) to an alkene proceeds with one halogen atom acting as an electrophile and the other as a nucleophile.

back_blocks.md: The alcohol is reacted with **SOCl**<sub>**2**</sub> (thionyl chloride). The reaction replaces the –OH group with –Cl to form the **chloroalkane**, releasing SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl as by-products.

front_blocks.md: Define **nucleophilic substitution**.

back_blocks.md: **Nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which a **nucleophile** attacks a carbon atom carrying a δ<sup>+</sup> charge, replacing the atom or group carrying a δ<sup>-</sup> charge (the **leaving group**).

front_blocks.md: What product is formed when a halogenoalkane reacts with ethanolic KCN under reflux, and why is this reaction useful?

back_blocks.md: A **nitrile** is formed (e.g. bromoethane + KCN → propanenitrile). The reaction is useful because it adds one **extra carbon atom** to the chain, extending the carbon skeleton of the starting material.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The hydroxide ion is a better nucleophile than water because it carries a full formal negative charge.

back_blocks.md: **True.** OH<sup>-</sup> has a **full negative charge**, making it a stronger nucleophile than water, where the oxygen only has a **partial negative charge** (δ<sup>-</sup>). Nucleophilic substitution with OH<sup>-</sup> is therefore much faster than with water.

front_blocks.md: Why must ammonia be used in excess in the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane?

back_blocks.md: The primary amine product (e.g. ethylamine) can itself act as a **nucleophile** and attack another halogenoalkane molecule, forming a **secondary amine** (e.g. diethylamine). Excess NH<sub>3</sub> minimises this over-substitution.

front_blocks.md: Define **hydrolysis**.

back_blocks.md: **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a molecule by **water**. In the context of halogenoalkanes, it refers to nucleophilic substitution by water (or OH<sup>-</sup>) to produce an **alcohol** and a halide ion.

front_blocks.md: How can aqueous silver nitrate be used to identify which halogen is present in a halogenoalkane?

back_blocks.md: Water in the AgNO<sub>3</sub> solution **hydrolyses** the halogenoalkane, releasing halide ions. These react with Ag<sup>+</sup> to form **coloured precipitates**: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) or AgI (yellow). The rate of precipitate formation also indicates bond strength.

front_blocks.md: Define **S****<sub>N</sub>****2 mechanism**.

front_blocks.md: Which type of halogenoalkane undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions, and why?

back_blocks.md: **Tertiary** halogenoalkanes undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions because the three alkyl groups stabilise the **tertiary carbocation** intermediate through the **inductive effect**, making the C–X bond easier to break in the slow rate-determining step.

front_blocks.md: Why does a primary halogenoalkane not form a primary carbocation as an intermediate in nucleophilic substitution?

back_blocks.md: A **primary carbocation** is much less stable than a tertiary carbocation because it has only **one alkyl group** donating electron density via the inductive effect. Primary halogenoalkanes therefore follow the S<sub>N</sub>2 pathway, avoiding the unstable primary carbocation.

front_blocks.md: Why do iodoalkanes react faster in nucleophilic substitution reactions than fluoroalkanes?

back_blocks.md: The C–I bond has a **lower bond energy** (228 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) than the C–F bond (467 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), so it requires less energy to break. The weaker C–I bond is therefore more easily broken during nucleophilic substitution.

front_blocks.md: In aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, iodoalkanes form a **..........** precipitate (AgI) most **..........** because C–I is the weakest C–X bond.

back_blocks.md: In aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, iodoalkanes form a **yellow** precipitate (AgI) most **rapidly** because C–I is the weakest C–X bond.

front_blocks.md: Define **aqueous silver nitrate test**.

back_blocks.md: An **aqueous silver nitrate test** is a method that identifies the halogen in a halogenoalkane by hydrolysing it and observing the colour of the silver halide **precipitate** formed: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) or AgI (yellow). The rate of formation also indicates reactivity.

front_blocks.md: Why is bond energy, rather than bond polarity, used to explain the reactivity trend in halogenoalkanes?

back_blocks.md: Although C–F is the most polar bond, **bond energy** governs reactivity here. The C–F bond is so **strong** (467 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) that it resists heterolytic fission, making fluoroalkanes unreactive despite their polarity.
